actions.name: Home blood pressure/heart rate log review
actions.result: Home readings over past 3 days: 102/58 HR 92, 98/60 HR 96, 105/62 HR 88 (seated). Standing BP today 86/52, HR 108, patient reports lightheadedness within 30 seconds of standing. Afebrile.

actions.name: Weight check (home scale)
actions.result: 132 lb today vs 138 lb at discharge 6 days ago (4.3% loss over 6 days). Patient reports oral intake was near-normal for the first several days after discharge and only declined to about one-third of usual over the past 2 days, so the full 6-lb loss is not explained by poor intake alone; the discrepancy suggests additional fluid loss (e.g., diuretic effect from self-resumed hydrochlorothiazide) contributing to volume depletion.

actions.name: Camera inspection - general appearance and mucous membranes
actions.result: Appears mildly fatigued but alert and oriented. Dry oral mucosa noted on camera. No visible edema on lower legs when patient lifts pant legs to camera. No rash.

actions.name: Patient self-exam - skin turgor (back of hand pinch test, demonstrated by video)
actions.result: Patient pinches skin on back of hand per instruction; tenting noted lasting ~3 seconds before recoil, consistent with reduced skin turgor.

actions.name: Jugular venous assessment via camera (patient reclined at 30-45 degrees, neck exposed)
actions.result: Neck veins not visibly distended; JVP estimated low/flat, difficult to assess precisely by video.

actions.name: Review discharge summary medication instructions
actions.result: Discharge summary dated 6 days ago: 'HOLD lisinopril 20mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25mg daily, and metformin 1000mg twice daily until follow-up labs confirm renal recovery and outpatient provider clears resumption. Continue other home medications as prescribed.' Signed by discharging hospitalist.

actions.name: Review current pharmacy fill/refill history
actions.result: Lisinopril 20mg last filled 34 days ago (90-day supply, pre-dating admission). Hydrochlorothiazide 25mg last filled 34 days ago. Metformin 1000mg last filled 34 days ago. No new fills logged since discharge.

actions.name: Repeat basic metabolic panel (yesterday, outpatient lab)
actions.result: See lab report: Creatinine 1.7 mg/dL (H), potassium 5.3 mmol/L (H), sodium 138 mmol/L, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L (L), BUN 38 mg/dL (H), glucose 142 mg/dL (H), eGFR 31 mL/min/1.73m2 (L). Calculated anion gap = 138-100-20 = 18 mmol/L (H, reference 8-12). This mild elevated anion-gap component, together with the low bicarbonate, is most consistent with uremic/renal acidosis given the markedly reduced eGFR (31); it is not specific for lactic acidosis. Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare but metformin should still be held given eGFR <45, as accumulation risk rises with worsening renal function - a lactate level should be checked if the patient develops worsening acidosis, tachypnea, or clinical deterioration.

actions.name: Order repeat BMP today (STAT outpatient or send to ED if critical)
actions.result: Ordered; pending - recommend urgent same-day draw given hyperkalemia and symptomatic orthostasis. Consider ED referral if patient unable to get same-day labs or if symptoms worsen.

actions.name: 12-lead ECG (home ECG patch or nearest facility, reviewed in record)
actions.result: ECG performed at outpatient lab draw site: sinus rhythm, rate 94, no peaked T waves, QRS 92ms, no significant interval changes from prior. No acute changes concerning for hyperkalemia-related conduction abnormality at this time.

actions.name: Review hospital discharge creatinine trend
actions.result: Admission creatinine 1.6 mg/dL, peak 2.1 mg/dL on day 3, discharge creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Documented baseline (6 months prior outpatient) 0.9 mg/dL.

actions.name: Review current full medication list as patient is actually taking it
actions.result: Patient-reported current intake: lisinopril 20mg daily (resumed self 2 days ago), hydrochlorothiazide 25mg daily (resumed self 2 days ago), metformin 1000mg twice daily (resumed self 2 days ago), ibuprofen 400mg up to three times daily for back pain (ongoing, not held), amlodipine 5mg daily (continued per discharge), atorvastatin 40mg nightly (continued per discharge).

actions.name: Dietary/oral intake recall (patient-reported, past 48 hours)
actions.result: Patient reports eating about one-third of usual meals, drinking roughly 3 cups of fluid daily (down from usual 6-8), no vomiting, mild nausea, decreased appetite since discharge.

actions.name: Urine output and color recall (patient-reported)
actions.result: Patient reports urinating less frequently than usual, urine described as 'darker, like weak tea' for the past 2 days.

actions.name: Pulse oximetry (home device)
actions.result: SpO2 97% on room air, no respiratory distress reported.

actions.name: Review discharge chest X-ray report
actions.result: Chest X-ray at discharge: Improving right lower lobe consolidation compared to admission film, no effusion. Findings consistent with resolving pneumonia.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Recurrent/worsening acute kidney injury with hyperkalemia due to inappropriate self-resumption of lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and ongoing NSAID (ibuprofen) use in the setting of volume depletion (poor oral intake over the past 2 days plus likely diuretic-driven losses, and orthostatic hypotension) during recovery from AKI after CAP - a 'triple whammy' nephrotoxic combination.
differential: Prerenal AKI from volume depletion (poor intake plus self-resumed diuretic) plus ACE-inhibitor/diuretic/NSAID triple-whammy effect (most likely)
Recurrent/unresolved AKI from pneumonia-related sepsis or acute tubular injury not yet fully recovered
Hyperkalemia from decreased renal clearance alone without medication contribution (less likely given temporal correlation with self-resumption)
Orthostatic hypotension from autonomic causes or over-diuresis independent of renal function (less likely as primary driver)
New cardiac arrhythmia from hyperkalemia (ruled out by reassuring ECG today but requires close monitoring)
keyFindings: Discharge summary explicitly held lisinopril, HCTZ, and metformin pending outpatient clearance
Patient restarted all three medications from old pill bottles 2 days before this visit, plus continued ibuprofen that was never held

Repeat labs show creatinine rising again (1.7 from discharge 1.4, against baseline 0.9) with new hyperkalemia (K 5.3) and a mild elevated anion-gap metabolic acidosis (bicarb 20, anion gap 18), most consistent with uremic/renal acidosis given eGFR 31 rather than established lactic acidosis
Symptomatic orthostatic hypotension (102/58 sitting dropping to 86/52 standing, HR rising to 108) consistent with volume depletion, compounded by self-resumed HCTZ
6-lb (4.3%) weight loss over 6 days is larger than expected from the 2 days of poor oral intake alone, suggesting an additional diuretic-driven fluid loss contributing to volume depletion

Pharmacy refill history shows no new fills for lisinopril, HCTZ, or metformin since 34 days ago (predating discharge), consistent with the patient taking medication from pre-admission stock rather than a fresh discharge-reconciled prescription
plan: Instruct patient to stop lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and ibuprofen immediately today; hold metformin given reduced eGFR (31) and accumulation risk, checking a lactate if clinical signs of lactic acidosis develop

Arrange urgent same-day repeat BMP given K 5.3 and symptomatic hypotension; given today's values and symptoms, strongly consider same-day in-person evaluation or ED referral for IV fluids and hyperkalemia management given symptomatic orthostasis and inability to safely rehydrate orally at home
Advise oral rehydration as tolerated while awaiting labs; hold diuretic and antihypertensives until renal function and volume status recover

Arrange close follow-up (24-48 hours) with repeat BMP once medications held and hydration improved; do not resume held medications without explicit confirmation from the treating physician and repeat labs showing renal recovery toward baseline (~0.9 mg/dL)

Perform medication reconciliation with patient and family/caregiver; involve son's household in confirming only the current approved medication list is accessible (consider removing or clearly labeling old bottles)

Communicate with patient's pharmacy to flag held medications and prevent further confusion from refill reminders; coordinate with primary care or discharging team regarding safe resumption timeline for ACE inhibitor and diuretic once stable
Reinforce that NSAIDs (ibuprofen) should be avoided entirely given current and recent renal impairment; discuss alternative pain management for back pain
Escalate for same-day evaluation (telehealth role should not manage symptomatic hyperkalemia and orthostatic hypotension purely remotely) - recommend ED or urgent in-person visit today
redFlags: Potassium 5.3 mmol/L with symptomatic orthostatic hypotension - risk for arrhythmia, warrants urgent escalation despite reassuring ECG
Standing BP 86/52 with HR 108 and lightheadedness - risk of falls, syncope, further prerenal injury
Creatinine trending back up (1.4 to 1.7) with eGFR 31 - ongoing kidney injury, not yet recovered to baseline

Mild elevated anion-gap metabolic acidosis (bicarb 20, anion gap 18) most consistent with uremic acidosis given eGFR 31; metformin should remain held and lactate checked if clinical deterioration occurs
Continued NSAID use in setting of recent and current AKI - avoid entirely
If patient becomes unable to tolerate oral fluids, develops chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or labs worsen further, needs immediate in-person/ED evaluation
educationPoints: The 'triple whammy' of ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic + NSAID significantly increases AKI risk, especially during volume depletion or recovery from a renal insult
Discharge medication reconciliation must explicitly address medications that were held, not just those that were started or changed, especially when patients have access to old pill bottles at home

An elevated anion gap with low bicarbonate in a patient with eGFR 31 is most consistent with uremic/renal acidosis; metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare and should not be presumed from this pattern alone, but metformin should still be held when eGFR is reduced due to accumulation risk, with lactate checked if clinical suspicion arises
Orthostatic vital sign assessment can be performed via telehealth using sequential home BP/HR readings in different positions and is an important part of a post-discharge AKI follow-up

When an acute weight change is larger than reported intake changes would explain, consider additional contributors (e.g., a resumed diuretic) rather than attributing the entire loss to poor oral intake

High health literacy and pride in self-management (a retired nurse) can paradoxically increase risk if the patient's knowledge is outdated or she bypasses current instructions, underscoring the need for explicit, non-judgmental confirmation of actual medication-taking behavior rather than assuming understanding equals adherence

artifacts.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
artifacts.author: Dr. Angela Reyes, Hospital Medicine
artifacts.body:
ADMISSION DIAGNOSIS: Community-acquired pneumonia, right lower lobe.
SECONDARY DIAGNOSIS: Acute kidney injury, likely prerenal/ATN overlap in setting of sepsis and poor intake.

HOSPITAL COURSE: Ms. Santos, 78yo woman, presented with 3 days of cough, fever, and malaise. Admitted for IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone then transitioned to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate) for CAP. Found to have AKI with creatinine rising from unknown baseline to peak 2.1 mg/dL on hospital day 3; prior outpatient baseline confirmed at 0.9 mg/dL from records 6 months prior. AKI attributed to combination of sepsis-related hypoperfusion, poor oral intake, and continued home ACE inhibitor/diuretic/NSAID use prior to admission. These medications were held during admission with improvement in renal function to 1.4 mg/dL by discharge. Clinically improved respiratory status; discharge chest X-ray showing improving consolidation.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS - MEDICATIONS:
HOLD the following until outpatient follow-up confirms renal recovery and primary care/nephrology clears resumption:
- Lisinopril 20mg daily (HELD)
- Hydrochlorothiazide 25mg daily (HELD)
- Metformin 1000mg twice daily (HELD - also check renal function given reduced eGFR)
CONTINUE:
- Amlodipine 5mg daily
- Atorvastatin 40mg nightly
- Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875mg twice daily x 2 more days to complete course
AVOID NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) given recent AKI.

FOLLOW-UP: Repeat basic metabolic panel in 5-7 days, telehealth follow-up with internal medicine within 1 week.

facts.chart: Patient presents for scheduled post-discharge follow-up after recent hospitalization for pneumonia and kidney problems; reports feeling weak and dizzy at home.
facts.says: I'm here for my follow-up after the hospital. I've just been feeling weak and a little dizzy when I stand up, but otherwise I think I'm doing okay.

facts.chart: Hospitalized 6 days ago x5 days for pneumonia with AKI, creatinine peaked 2.1.
facts.says: I was in the hospital for pneumonia, and they told me my kidneys got a little upset too, but they said it was getting better before I left.

facts.chart: Reports generalized weakness and fatigue since discharge, worse than expected for recovery stage.
facts.says: I just don't have much energy. More than I'd expect just getting over pneumonia.

facts.chart: Lightheadedness occurs specifically on standing, resolves with sitting; occurring for about 2 days.
facts.says: It's mainly when I stand up fast, like from the bed or a chair. The room sort of spins for a second and I have to sit right back down.

facts.chart: Patient restarted lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and metformin from pre-admission bottles 2 days ago without consulting the care team.
facts.says: I know my own medicines - I've been a nurse for forty years. Once I started feeling a bit better, I just went back to taking my regular pills like before. I know what I need.

facts.chart: Patient recalls being told something about holding medications but believed it was only temporary during the hospital stay, not something to continue after discharge.
facts.says: They did say something about not taking a couple of my pills while I was in there, but I figured that was just for while I was in the hospital. Once I was home and felt stronger, I thought it made sense to go back to normal.

facts.chart: Continues ibuprofen 400mg up to 3 times daily for chronic back pain; never stopped it, including during hospitalization.
facts.says: Oh, I never stopped my ibuprofen. My back has been bad for years, I need that just to get through the day. I don't think anyone told me to stop that one.

facts.chart: Oral intake near-normal for the first ~4 days after discharge, then decreased over the past 2 days to about a third of usual meals with reduced fluid intake; mild nausea, no vomiting.
facts.says: I was eating pretty normally the first few days home, but the last couple of days I haven't had much appetite - maybe a third of what I usually eat. Nothing tastes right and I feel a little sick to my stomach sometimes.

facts.chart: Reports decreased urinary frequency and darker urine for past 2 days.
facts.says: Now that you mention it, I haven't been going to the bathroom as much, and when I do, it's darker, kind of like weak tea.

facts.chart: Denies fever, chills, or recurrence of cough/sputum production since discharge.
facts.says: No fever, no chills. My cough is pretty much gone now.

facts.chart: Denies chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath.
facts.says: No chest pain, no racing heart that I've noticed, and I'm not short of breath.

facts.chart: Denies any falls, but reports near-fall yesterday when standing quickly, caught herself on dresser.
facts.says: I almost fell yesterday morning - I grabbed onto my dresser just in time. Scared me a little.

facts.chart: History of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, chronic low back pain (degenerative disc disease).
facts.says: I've got my high blood pressure, my sugar, my cholesterol, and this old back of mine.

facts.chart: Continues amlodipine 5mg daily and atorvastatin 40mg nightly as instructed; completed amoxicillin-clavulanate course as prescribed.
facts.says: I'm still taking my amlodipine and my cholesterol pill every day like they told me, and I finished the rest of my antibiotic.

facts.chart: Lives with son, daughter-in-law, and two grandchildren in Daly City; son helps with some tasks but patient manages her own medications independently.
facts.says: I live with my son and his family. They're wonderful, but I handle my own pills - always have. I don't want to be a burden.

facts.chart: Patient is a retired nurse, takes pride in medical knowledge and self-management; may be reluctant to accept that her understanding is outdated.
facts.says: I was a nurse for over forty years at this same hospital system, you know. I know how to take care of myself and manage my medications.

facts.chart: Expresses concern about becoming a burden to her son's family or losing independence if her health worsens.
facts.says: I don't want my son's family to have to take care of me like I'm helpless. I've always been the one taking care of others.

facts.chart: Confirms she kept her previous prescription bottles (lisinopril, HCTZ, metformin) at home rather than disposing of them after discharge instructions.
facts.says: I still had the bottles from before in my medicine cabinet, so I just started back up with those once I felt ready.

facts.chart: Patient aware repeat labs were drawn yesterday but has not yet been told the results prior to this visit.
facts.says: I went in for blood work yesterday like they told me, but nobody's called me with the results yet.

facts.chart: Denies leg or ankle swelling.
facts.says: No swelling in my legs or feet that I've noticed.

facts.chart: Denies confusion, memory changes, or difficulty concentrating.
facts.says: My mind feels clear, no confusion or memory trouble.

facts.chart: Denies alcohol use and tobacco use, never smoked.
facts.says: I don't drink alcohol and I've never smoked.

facts.chart: Family history notable for hypertension and type 2 diabetes in mother and sister; no known kidney disease in family.
facts.says: My mother and sister both had high blood pressure and sugar problems, but nobody in the family had kidney trouble that I know of.

facts.chart: Reports chronic low back pain rated 5/10 currently, longstanding, uses ibuprofen as primary management, has not tried other therapies recently.
facts.says: My back pain is about a 5 out of 10 most days. The ibuprofen is really the only thing that's worked well for me.

facts.chart: Normally follows a rice-based Filipino diet with moderate portions; reports no significant dietary changes related to diabetes management recently, blood sugar logs not available today.
facts.says: I eat my usual rice and vegetables, fish sometimes. I haven't been checking my sugar as much since I've been so tired.

facts.chart: Able to ambulate independently at baseline; since discharge requires holding onto furniture or walls when moving around due to weakness and dizziness.
facts.says: I used to just walk around fine, but now I'm holding onto the walls and furniture to get around the house.

facts.chart: Expresses some frustration that discharge instructions were confusing or that she felt rushed at discharge.
facts.says: Honestly, when I left the hospital, it was all a bit of a blur. They gave me a lot of papers and I was just so happy to be going home, I didn't read everything carefully.

facts.chart: Hopes to be told she is recovering well and can return to her normal routine and medication regimen soon.
facts.says: I'm hoping you'll tell me I'm on the mend and can just get back to my normal routine.

facts.chart: No relevant sexual health concerns raised; not pertinent to this visit.
facts.says: That's not really something that comes up for me at this point in my life.

facts.chart: Reports mild generalized muscle weakness, denies focal weakness, denies muscle cramps.
facts.says: My muscles just feel weak all over, nothing in particular, no cramping though.

facts.chart: No known drug allergies.
facts.says: No allergies to any medications that I know of.

facts.chart: Son is aware she is taking her usual pills again but has not reviewed the discharge paperwork in detail himself.
facts.says: My son knows I'm back on my regular pills. He hasn't gone through all that discharge paperwork himself - he trusts me to handle it.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes resuming her usual lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and metformin was appropriate once she felt stronger, stating she knows her own medications from 40 years of nursing experience.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Discharge summary explicitly states these three medications were to be HELD until outpatient follow-up confirmed renal recovery and the primary care/nephrology team cleared resumption - not restarted based on how she felt.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient's professional background and confidence can create a false sense of security about self-managing medication changes; explicit, written discharge instructions must be reviewed and reinforced regardless of a patient's health literacy or clinical background, since 'held' medications require specific clearance, not symptom-based self-assessment.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she doesn't think anyone told her to stop the ibuprofen and has continued taking it for chronic back pain throughout and after her hospitalization.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Discharge summary explicitly lists 'AVOID NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) given recent AKI' as a specific instruction.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may selectively recall or miss instructions bundled with multiple other discharge points, especially around medications they consider separate from their 'main' prescriptions (like an over-the-counter pain reliever); medication reconciliation should explicitly ask about all substances including OTC/NSAIDs, not just prescribed chronic disease medications.

objectives.text: Elicit through history that the patient has self-resumed held nephrotoxic/renally-cleared medications (lisinopril, HCTZ, metformin) and continued NSAID use, recognizing the discrepancy between discharge instructions and actual home medication-taking behavior.
Identify symptomatic orthostatic hypotension and volume depletion through history and remote vital sign assessment (home BP log, standing vitals, intake/output history).
Interpret trending renal function and electrolyte labs to recognize recurrent AKI with hyperkalemia and connect this to the medication and volume status findings.
Recognize the 'triple whammy' nephrotoxic combination (ACE inhibitor + diuretic + NSAID) in the context of volume depletion and reduced renal function, and generate an appropriate differential.

Formulate a safe, in-scope management plan that holds offending medications, arranges urgent reassessment/escalation given hyperkalemia and symptomatic hypotension, and addresses the mismatch between the patient's self-management beliefs and documented instructions with sensitivity to her professional identity and desire for independence.

Explore psychosocial context (pride in independence, prior nursing career, concern about burdening family, confusion at discharge) to understand barriers to adherence without being judgmental, and involve family/caregiver appropriately in medication safety.

patient.name: Gloria Santos
patient.language: English (primary), fluent; occasionally uses Tagalog terms with family
patient.appearance: An elderly woman with gray hair pulled back neatly, sitting upright in a cardigan on a couch in a tidy, well-lit living room. She appears mildly fatigued, with slightly sunken eyes, but maintains good eye contact and a composed, dignified demeanor throughout the call.

persona.personality: Proud, articulate, and self-assured, with a strong sense of personal competence rooted in her nursing career; warm but can be subtly defensive when her judgment is questioned.
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and organized in describing symptoms, uses some clinical vocabulary accurately but applies it to outdated practices; polite and respectful, occasionally minimizes symptoms to appear capable.
persona.emotionalState: Mildly anxious about her weakness and dizziness but trying to appear composed and in control; slightly embarrassed when the medication issue is raised.
persona.background: Worked as a registered nurse for over 40 years at a local hospital before retiring 8 years ago. Immigrated from the Philippines in her twenties. Widowed 5 years ago, now lives with her son's family in Daly City, helping with grandchildren when she can. Enjoys cooking, gardening, and watching Filipino drama series with her daughter-in-law.
speechExamples: I was a nurse for over forty years, I think I know how to take care of myself.
It's nothing serious, just a little spell when I stand up too fast.
I didn't want to bother anyone by calling about the dizziness - I figured it would pass.
My son's family does so much for me already, I don't want to add to their plate.
I suppose I thought once I was feeling stronger, it made sense to just go back to my normal pills.
concerns: I'm just feeling weak and dizzy—is this normal after pneumonia, or is something else going on?
I've been taking my regular medicines because I know what I need, but now I'm worried I did something wrong.
I don't want to go back to the hospital or be a burden on my son's family—can we just fix this at home?
Why are my kidneys acting up again? I thought I was getting better when they sent me home.

scenario.studentBrief: You are seeing Gloria Santos, a 78-year-old woman, for a scheduled telehealth post-discharge follow-up. She was hospitalized 6 days ago for 5 days with community-acquired pneumonia complicated by acute kidney injury (creatinine peaked at 2.1 mg/dL, baseline 0.9 mg/dL, discharge 1.4 mg/dL). Several home medications were held at discharge pending outpatient clearance. Conduct a focused interview and remote assessment, review her available records and labs, and determine next steps.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Weakness and lightheadedness on standing since hospital discharge for pneumonia and acute kidney injury
scenario.openingLine: Hi doctor, thanks for seeing me. I'm here for my follow-up after the hospital. I've just been feeling weak and a little dizzy when I stand up, but otherwise I think I'm doing okay.
tasks: Take a focused history of the presenting concern
Review available laboratory results and vital signs
Formulate an assessment and plan, including disposition
Communicate findings and next steps with the patient

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in her son's living room in Daly City, California
profile.summary: A 78-year-old retired nurse presents for post-discharge follow-up after pneumonia complicated by AKI, having self-resumed held medications (lisinopril, HCTZ, metformin) and continued NSAID use, now with recurrent AKI, hyperkalemia, and symptomatic orthostatic hypotension from volume depletion. The case teaches recognition of the 'triple whammy' nephrotoxic medication combination, remote assessment of volume status, and sensitive medication reconciliation with a patient whose professional identity complicates acceptance of updated instructions.
profile.title: Post-Discharge Follow-Up After Pneumonia and AKI: Self-Resumed Medications and Recurrent Kidney Injury
